evidence: gpt-oss-120b explicitly partitions jobs with "if d1 <= d2" and "if d1 > d2", then uses "list1.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])", "list2.sort(key=lambda x: -x[1])", and concatenates them.
affordance_in_statement: On the Primary Axis, lenses are placed one after another in your chosen sequence without overlapping; for any given lens, its Secondary Axis clearance must start physically at or after the coordinate where its own Primary Axis clearance ends; on the Secondary Axis, lenses are placed one after another in the exact same chosen sequence without overlapping.
secondary_shortcut_name: direct recognition of Johnson's ordering rule
removal_suggestion: Preserve the same inequalities and objective, but re-present them as an indirect coupled-coordinate geometry problem rather than explicitly describing two axes as sequential stages using the exact same permutation. Avoid the textbook flow-shop terminology and distribute the dependency conditions through the scenario description.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes the problem as a two-machine permutation flow-shop problem and applies Johnson's rule: ascending d1 for d1 <= d2, followed by descending d2 for d1 > d2.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The two clearances are processed sequentially on separate axes in the same chosen sequence, with the secondary start constrained by completion of the primary clearance.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: It sorts every lens only by d1 ascending, ignoring the required partition into d1 <= d2 and d1 > d2 cases.
It uses the same incorrect global d1-ascending ordering, despite calling it a known greedy strategy.
It sorts by d1 descending and computes a suffix maximum of d1 + d2, which is not the optimal permutation rule for this coupled scheduling objective.

recommended_edit: Make one presentation edit: replace the explicit Primary/Secondary sequential-axis bullets with an indirect geometric dependency description that preserves all three coordinate inequalities and the final-boundary objective, but does not visibly expose the standard two-machine same-permutation flow-shop pattern.
